title: Compile Time and Runtime
summary: Understand when TypeScript checks your code, what happens during execution, and why runtime validation remains necessary.

body.raw:
Compile time and runtime describe different stages in a program's lifecycle. Understanding the distinction explains why code can pass TypeScript checks and still fail when it receives real data. ## Compile time Compilation transforms source code into another representation. For TypeScript, this commonly means producing JavaScript. Type checking evaluates the program's declared types and how values are used. The TypeScript compiler can report invalid syntax, unknown identifiers, and incompatible types. These diagnostics help developers catch problems before deployment: ```typescript const attempts: number = "three"; // Type error: a string is not assignable to a number. ``` Compilation and type checking are not always the same step. Some tools remove TypeScript syntax without checking types. A build pipeline should run an explicit type check, such as `tsc --noEmit`, when its transpiler does not provide one. Compiler settings also determine whether JavaScript can be emitted despite diagnostics. ## Runtime Runtime is the period in which the program executes. JavaScript runs in an engine within a browser, Node.js, or another host. Execution can happen on a server, in a background worker, or during a build as well as during a user's session. Real inputs and environmental conditions become relevant at this stage. Network requests can fail, configuration can be missing, and an API can return an unexpected value: ```javascript const user = { email: null }; console.log(user.email.toUpperCase()); // Runtime TypeError: null has no toUpperCase method. ``` ## How the stages compare
AspectCompile timeRuntime
ActivityTransforming source and checking declared typesExecuting the program with actual inputs
Typical toolsTypeScript compiler and build toolsJavaScript engine and its host environment
Typical failuresInvalid syntax, unknown names, incompatible typesNetwork failures, invalid data, unavailable resources
ImpactCan block a build when checks are enforcedCan interrupt a request, job, or user interaction
ControlsType checking and build validationInput validation, error handling, and monitoring
## Why both types and validation matter A TypeScript interface describes an assumption about a value; it does not inspect incoming JSON. A runtime schema checks that value before code uses it. Combine static checking with boundary validation, then handle operational failures separately. For example, a correctly typed request can still time out. A valid JSON response can still contain the wrong fields. A response that matches a schema can still violate a business rule that the schema does not express. ## Practical workflow 1. Define the expected data model and enable appropriate TypeScript checks. 2. Run type checking before deployment. 3. Treat external inputs as untrusted until they have been validated. 4. Handle network, parsing, and validation failures with an intentional fallback. 5. Monitor failures during execution so production issues are visible. ## Further reading - [TypeScript handbook on checking, emitting, and erased types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/basic-types.html) - [Zod and runtime validation](/knowledge/zod-runtime-validation)
